posted_prompt: A concise 2D animation illustrates an array of numbered boxes arranged horizontally (e.g., [5, 1, 2, 4, 3]), with a highlighted pointer moving from left to right to perform a sequential search for a target value (e.g., 4).
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Sequential search, a deterministic, linear, index-ordered traversal algorithm that compares elements one-by-one until first match. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: (1) array is static and unsorted; (2) search proceeds strictly left-to-right by index; (3) termination occurs immediately upon equality detection; (4) no implicit memory or backtracking. Phased storyline: [Phase 1: Static setup. Array [5,1,2,4,3] and "Target: 4" banner displayed.] → [Phase 2: Initiation. Pointer appears at index 0 (5), pulses, compares "5==4? → false".] → [Phase 3: Iteration. Pointer advances to 1→2→4, each with identical compare-false feedback.] → [Phase 4: Termination. Pointer lands on 4, triggers synchronous green pulse + "4==4" confirmation + "FOUND" badge.] → [Phase 5: Completion. Animation holds final state for ≥0.5s. Visibility constraints: All numbers and pointer must be legible at native resolution; no occlusion; perspective is strict 2D front-facing orthographic view; no camera motion or zoom.
manual:
I. Basic Demonstration Information
Demonstration Title: Sequential Search Algorithm Execution Process Demonstration
Subject: Engineering - Computer Science - Algorithms
Demonstration Purpose: To visually demonstrate the step-by-step execution of the sequential search algorithm on a fixed-size array, highlighting the left-to-right traversal pattern, element-by-element comparison, and termination upon first match; to reinforce understanding of linear time complexity and deterministic control flow.
II. Demonstration Carrier/Equipment
Core Carrier: 2D animated schematic — horizontal row of 5 uniformly sized, bordered, rectangular boxes containing integers [5, 1, 2, 4, 3]; a movable pointer (e.g., downward-pointing red triangle); persistent target indicator (e.g., banner "Target: 4").
Auxiliary Equipment: Clean white or light-gray background; sans-serif numeric labels (size ≥24pt, high contrast); frame rate ≥30fps; total duration ≤10s.
III. Demonstration Content Description
Layout: Array centered horizontally; pointer begins aligned with leftmost box (value 5); target banner placed above array.
State Control: Pointer advances strictly left-to-right, one box per step; dwell time per box = 0.6s; upon reaching value 4 (third box from right, index 3), pointer pauses 0.8s while matched box pulses green and displays "MATCH!"
Comparison Baseline: All boxes identical in size, spacing, fill (white), border (black, 2px), and font; only numeric content and pointer state vary.
IV. Observation of Core Phenomena
Pointer Motion Pattern: Smooth, discrete, sequential translation — no interpolation errors, no skipping, no reversal.
Visual Comparison Feedback: At each box, a transient visual cue (e.g., subtle glow + tooltip "X == 4?") appears synchronously with pointer landing.
Match Confirmation: Exclusive, unambiguous response only at value 4 — green pulse + bold "4" + "FOUND" badge; no secondary effects elsewhere.
Characteristic Stability: Array geometry, label legibility, and pointer shape remain invariant throughout; no flicker, scaling, or color bleed.
V. Summary of Key Knowledge Points and Principles
Core Concept Definition: Sequential search is a brute-force algorithm that checks each element of a list in order until the target is found or the list ends; worst-case time complexity is O(n), best-case O(1).
Algorithmic Logic Visualization: The animation directly maps abstract pseudocode (FOR i = 0 TO n−1 DO IF A[i] == target THEN RETURN i) to observable states — position ↔ index, pulse ↔ comparison, green highlight ↔ return condition.
Pedagogical Significance: Reinforces procedural thinking, state tracking, and the importance of termination conditions; contrasts with binary search by emphasizing lack of ordering assumptions.

selected_point: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal Demonstration
posted_prompt: Display a simple binary tree on a light background, with nodes labeled (1–7); highlight the nodes from top to bottom according to their level using bright colors (e.g., red) to demonstrate level order traversal. Briefly illuminate each node when visited, and add a mark for it — its numeral if legible digits can be rendered, otherwise a simple tally mark or dot — to the left-to-right output list at the bottom of the screen.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Level order traversal as breadth-first, level-synchronized node visiting in a full binary tree.
Minimum mechanism: Tree structure must enforce parent–child relationships (1→2,3; 2→4,5; 3→6,7); illumination must be a discrete, transient visual event tied to visitation; the output list must grow incrementally and irreversibly via left-to-right append, one mark per visited node (a numeral is preferred where legible digit rendering is reliable; a simple tally mark or dot is an acceptable substitute).
(ii)Storyline: Frame 0: Static full binary tree (1–7) and empty output list on light background, all nodes unhighlighted.
→ Illumination of node 1 (red highlight appears, brief duration) → a mark for it appears in the output list.
→ Illumination of node 2 (red highlight appears) → a second mark appends to the right of the first.
→ Illumination of node 3 (red highlight appears) → a third mark appends.
→ Illumination of node 4 → a fourth mark appends.
→ Illumination of node 5 → a fifth mark appends.
→ Illumination of node 6 → a sixth mark appends.
→ Illumination of node 7 → a seventh mark appends.
All illuminations are mutually exclusive (only one node lit at a time), brief, and identical in visual character; the output list never deletes, overwrites, or rearranges its marks; viewpoint is fixed front-facing, no camera motion or zoom.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Display a full binary tree with 7 nodes labeled 1 (root), 2–3 (level 1), 4–7 (level 2), on a uniform light background.
2. Initialize an empty horizontal output list at the bottom of the screen.
3. Illuminate nodes one at a time in strict level order: node 1, then node 2, then node 3, then nodes 4, 5, 6, and 7 in that left-to-right order; each illumination is brief and visually distinct, with only one node lit at any moment.
4. As each node is illuminated, append a mark for it (its numeral, or a simple tally/dot if legible digits are not available) to the output list, left-to-right.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- A static full binary tree with labeled nodes 1–7 remains fixed on light background.
- Nodes illuminate one-by-one in level order (1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7), each with brief, bright, uniform highlight.

selected_point: Identification of Erythromycin Drugs (Sulfuric Acid Colorimetric Method)
posted_prompt: Transfer an appropriate amount of erythromycin reagent solution into a test tube. Slowly add concentrated sulfuric acid along the inner wall of the test tube using a pipette. Keep the test tube upright, gently shake to mix the contents, and observe the progress of the reaction inside the test tube.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Acid-induced chromogenic reaction of erythromycin in concentrated sulfuric acid, requiring interfacial contact, controlled mixing, and time-resolved color development.
Minimum mechanism: Erythromycin must be dissolved in aqueous medium; concentrated H₂SO₄ is fully miscible with the aqueous solution in all proportions but is much denser, so when it is added slowly along the tube wall it sinks and briefly forms a distinct lower layer rather than mixing instantly; reaction initiates at the acid–solution interface due to localized protonation/dehydration of erythromycin; color formation is diffusion-limited before shaking and requires mechanical agitation for homogenization.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 1–2: Upright empty test tube → Frame 3–4: Erythromycin solution added → Frame 5–6: Pipette contacts inner wall, acid begins flowing down → Frame 7: Distinct biphasic layering (upper aqueous, lower acid) visible → Frame 8: Reddish-brown band appears sharply at interface → Frame 9: Gentle shaking initiates → Frame 10: Color disperses upward continuously; final state is homogeneous reddish-brown. All events occur from fixed frontal viewpoint; tube remains fully in frame; no occlusion of interface or reaction zone; lighting remains constant to ensure visibility of color progression.

Experimental Procedure
1. Place a clean, dry test tube upright on bench.
2. Transfer erythromycin reagent solution into the tube (~1 mL).
3. Using a pipette, slowly dispense concentrated sulfuric acid along the inner wall of the tube.
4. Keep tube upright; gently shake to mix.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A reddish-brown or cherry-red color develops first at the acid–aqueous interface, then disperses upward during shaking to yield a uniform reddish-brown solution. No precipitate or gas forms.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Erythromycin undergoes dehydration and rearrangement in concentrated H₂SO₄, forming chromophoric compounds that absorb visible light in the red-orange region — basis of the sulfuric acid colorimetric identification method.

posted_prompt: On the green, a player gently strikes a golf ball with a putter, sending it rolling across the putting surface toward the hole.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Skid-to-roll transition of a golf ball following centered putter impact, governed by green surface friction and topography, culminating in complete hole entry.
Minimum mechanism: Putter impact typically imparts a brief initial skid: right after contact the ball's translational velocity does not yet match its angular velocity (v ≠ ωr) because of putter loft and impact dynamics; green-surface friction then acts on the skidding ball until true rolling (v = ωr) is established, generally within roughly the first 20–40% of its travel distance; from that point onward the ball must continue in pure rolling contact without further sliding, and the hole geometry must allow full submersion upon arrival.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–1] Putter held stationary behind ball on green; [Frame 2–3] Putt impact occurs: ball begins forward motion with a brief initial skid; [Frame 4–7] Ball transitions into and maintains continuous rolling contact with the green surface, keeping spherical form, progressing visibly toward hole; [Frame 8–9] Ball reaches hole rim, makes contact, and fully disappears below cup level; Perspective must be fixed (e.g., low-angle side or slightly elevated frontal view), ensuring all key events (impact, skid-to-roll transition, approach, entry) remain simultaneously visible and unoccluded throughout.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Position a white dimpled golf ball on a flat section of a well-manicured green.
2. Align a standard putter behind the ball, perpendicular to intended line.
3. Gently strike the ball center with the putter face to send it forward (a brief initial skid before rolling begins is expected).
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- The ball remains spherical and white throughout.
- Immediately after impact the ball briefly skids; green-surface friction then establishes continuous, ground-coupled rolling directed toward the hole.
- Apart from that brief initial skid, no bounce, hop, or airborne phase occurs.
- Ball enters the hole fully and disappears below the rim without rebound or protrusion.
Summary of Experimental Principles
A putting stroke applies centered, low-loft impact that first imparts a brief skid to the ball; green-surface friction converts this into pure rolling motion within roughly the first 20–40% of its path, after which the ball rolls under control toward the hole, decelerating predictably along the intended line.

selected_point: The triple jump stride rhythm is characterized by the sequence jump - leap - jump, referred to as the triple jump stride rhythm. The first step lands on the takeoff leg, the second step lands on the swinging leg, and the third step involves both feet landing simultaneously, exhibiting distinct stride characteristics.
posted_prompt: A long jumper sprints, takes off with one leg, completes a standard and complete triple jump, and lands with both feet in the sand pit. The entire movement is clearly and smoothly presented.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Triple jump as a rhythmically segmented horizontal jumping sequence governed by strict leg alternation and terminal symmetry.
Minimum mechanism: Human bipedal locomotion with unilateral force generation enabling three discrete, causally chained aerial phases, where each landing directly enables the next takeoff via elastic recoil and neuromuscular coordination; sand pit must serve as unambiguous, deformable endpoint confirming final bilateral impact.
(ii)Storyline: Sprint → single-leg takeoff → first flight → first contact (takeoff leg only) → second flight → second contact (swinging leg only) → third flight → third contact (both feet simultaneously in sand). Causal transitions require visible continuity: takeoff impulse determines first flight arc; first landing posture and timing enable second takeoff; second landing sets up final takeoff angle and height; final flight trajectory must descend into sand with bilateral foot alignment visible at frame of impact. Perspective must be frontal or oblique side view (not overhead or extreme low angle) to unambiguously resolve foot identity, contact timing, and sand interaction. All events occur in same continuous shot with fixed viewpoint and stable lighting.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Athlete sprints horizontally toward sand pit.
2. Takes off from one leg (takeoff leg) into first flight phase (jump).
3. Lands on same takeoff leg (first contact).
4. Immediately rebounds into second flight phase (leap), landing on opposite (swinging) leg (second contact).
5. Immediately rebounds into third flight phase (final jump), landing with both feet simultaneously in sand pit (third contact).
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
- First contact: single foot (takeoff leg) on ground.
- Second contact: single foot (swinging leg) on ground — opposite limb from first contact.
- Third contact: both feet touching sand at identical time — no stagger, no sequence.
- Flight-phase distances follow standard triple-jump proportions: the swinging-leg leap (step) phase is typically the shortest of the three, while the takeoff-leg jump and the final bilateral jump cover comparably longer distances.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Triple jump stride rhythm = jump (takeoff leg landing) → leap (swinging leg landing) → jump (bilateral landing); biomechanically defined by alternating leg dominance followed by symmetrical landing.

subject: Economics
selected_point: Draw a bar chart comparing various expenditures under a fiscal deficit.
posted_prompt: A set of axes is displayed on the screen, with the horizontal axis representing budget category and the vertical axis representing amount. Under conditions of fiscal deficit, a bar chart is created to represent income and expenditure.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Fiscal deficit as a visualizable relational condition, defined as "total government expenditure exceeds total government revenue" within a fixed accounting period. Minimum assumptions: (1) monetary amounts are quantifiable and comparable across budget categories; (2) bar height is a valid visual channel for magnitude comparison; (3) budget-category identity justifies separate, evenly spaced positions along the x-axis; (4) color coding (green=income, red-orange=expenditure) is used consistently and is perceptually distinguishable. Expected Phased Storyline: [Phase 1: Setup] Axes appear: horizontal axis labeled "Budget Category", vertical axis labeled "Amount". [Phase 2: Income Anchor] A green bar rises at the leftmost position, representing income/revenue. [Phase 3: Expenditure Bars] Three or more red-orange bars rise sequentially to the right, each one taller than the income bar, representing distinct expenditure categories that collectively exceed income. [Phase 4: Stable Deficit Signal] The final frame holds with the height difference between the income bar and expenditure bars clearly visible: no numbers, no annotations, no further motion. Visibility Constraints: legible at 1080p; no occlusion; axis labels readable without zooming; color contrast sufficient for the green and red-orange bars to be told apart; all bars fully within frame.
manual:
Fiscal Deficit Expenditure Bar Chart Demonstration Instructions
I. Basic Demonstration Information
Demonstration Title: Bar Chart Visualization of Income vs. Expenditure Under Fiscal Deficit Conditions
Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences — Economics — Public Finance
Demonstration Purpose: To visually demonstrate how a fiscal deficit manifests in a bar chart — specifically, by displaying income (revenue) and multiple categories of government expenditure on a shared coordinate system where the horizontal axis represents "Budget Category" (i.e., the distinct budget items being compared) and the vertical axis represents "Amount" (i.e., the monetary magnitude, serving as the quantitative scale). The chart must clearly show that total expenditure bars exceed the income bar, visually encoding deficit conditions. This supports conceptual understanding of fiscal imbalance, budgetary visualization literacy, and interpretation of public finance data.

II. Demonstration Carrier/Equipment
Core Carrier: Digital charting interface (e.g., clean vector-based 2D plotting environment with no gridlines or decorative elements unless specified); pre-defined dataset comprising one income value and ≥3 distinct expenditure categories (e.g., Education, Healthcare, Defense, Debt Servicing), where sum of expenditures > income.
Auxiliary Equipment: Neutral gray background (RGB 240,240,240); sans-serif font (e.g., Arial, 14pt); axis labels rendered in bold black text; consistent color-coding: income bar = green (#2E7D32), expenditure bars = red-orange gradient (#D32F2F → #EF6C00) to signal fiscal strain; optional subtle deficit annotation ("Deficit = Expenditure − Income") in bottom-right corner.

III. Demonstration Content Description
Layout: A single Cartesian coordinate system appears centered on screen. Horizontal (x) axis labeled "Budget Category" (aligned below axis, centered), vertical (y) axis labeled "Amount" (rotated 90°, aligned left of axis, centered). Both axes extend fully across visible plot area with tick marks but no numeric values shown (to emphasize structural relationship over precise quantification).
State Control: Chart renders in static, non-animated sequence: (1) axes appear first; (2) income bar drawn vertically at x=0 (leftmost position); (3) ≥3 expenditure bars drawn sequentially rightward (x=1, x=2, x=3…), all taller than income bar; (4) final frame holds for ≥2 seconds with clear visual dominance of red-orange expenditure bars over green income bar.
Comparison Baseline: All bars share identical width and spacing; y-axis scale is linear and consistent; no logarithmic scaling or distortion. Height difference between income and tallest expenditure bar is ≥30% of income height — ensuring deficit condition is perceptually unambiguous.

IV. Observation of Core Phenomena
Axes Appearance: A clean pair of orthogonal black lines forms the coordinate system. Horizontal line (x-axis) runs left-to-right, labeled "Budget Category"; vertical line (y-axis) runs bottom-to-top, labeled "Amount". No arrows, no origin marker "(0,0)", but orientation is unambiguous.
Income Bar: Single upright green rectangle, positioned at far-left (x=0), height proportional to revenue value. Uniform fill, no outline, no label on bar.
Expenditure Bars: ≥3 upright rectangles, positioned sequentially to the right of income bar (x=1,2,3), each in warm-toned red-orange hues. All are visibly taller than the green income bar. No overlapping, no stacking — side-by-side comparison only.
Deficit Visual Signal: The collective visual weight and vertical extent of red-orange bars dominate the frame; green bar appears comparatively short and isolated — creating immediate perceptual contrast confirming "expenditure > income".
Stability & Clarity: No flickering, no partial rendering, no occlusion. All elements remain static and fully legible throughout final display. Color contrast ratio (green vs. red-orange against gray background) exceeds WCAG AA standard (≥4.5:1) for accessibility.

V. Summary of Key Knowledge Points and Principles
Core Concept Definition: A fiscal deficit occurs when a government's total expenditures exceed its total revenues (excluding borrowing) within a given period. Visualizing this via comparative bar charts transforms abstract macroeconomic imbalance into an intuitive spatial relationship: longer bars = larger monetary outflows.
Principle of Visual Feature Recognition Comparison: The human visual system rapidly detects relative height differences in aligned vertical bars. By fixing the x-axis as "Budget Category" (a categorical axis identifying each budget item) and the y-axis as "Amount" (a quantitative axis measuring monetary magnitude), the chart enforces a direct, ordinal comparison. The deficit is not calculated numerically but recognized visually via height asymmetry — a standard convention in bar-chart design for comparing discrete categories against a shared numeric scale.
Further Knowledge: Real-world fiscal charts often include borrowing (deficit financing) as a separate bar or annotation; however, this demonstration isolates the core deficit condition (expenditure > revenue) without introducing secondary mechanisms. "Budget Category" (horizontal) and "Amount" (vertical) follow the standard categorical-axis/quantitative-axis convention used in most bar charts, so a viewer familiar with ordinary bar charts can read the chart without any special training.

VI. Demonstration Precautions
Axis Label Fidelity: "Budget Category" must appear only on the horizontal axis; "Amount" only on the vertical axis — swapping labels invalidates the demonstration. Font size and weight must ensure legibility at standard viewing distance.
Color Semantics: Green must exclusively represent income; red-orange hues must exclusively represent expenditures. Use of blue, purple, or gray for any bar constitutes misrepresentation of fiscal signaling conventions.
Bar Count Minimum: Exactly one income bar + at least three distinct expenditure bars required. Two expenditure bars or zero expenditure bars fails the "various expenditures" requirement.
Temporal Integrity: Axes must render before any bars. Bars must appear in left-to-right order (income → expenditure1 → expenditure2 → …). No simultaneous pop-in or randomized order.
No Extraneous Elements: No titles, legends, data values, gridlines, animations, or sound. Chart must be minimal, pedagogically focused, and self-contained.

posted_prompt: Outdoors in a gentle breeze, with a wind indicator such as nearby grass or a hanging fabric ribbon visibly swaying to mark the wind, two identically configured microphones are mounted side by side and face the same direction as gusts pass through: one microphone is left fully exposed, the other is enclosed in a thick foam windscreen. (i) Target concept: Aerodynamic damping of airborne pressure fluctuations via porous medium.

manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Mount two identical microphones side-by-side on fixed stands outdoors.
2. Leave left microphone fully exposed; fit right microphone with thick, opaque foam windscreen covering entire grille.
3. Orient both microphones identically, facing into gentle breeze.
4. Record 10 seconds as wind gusts pass through scene.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Exposed microphone grille visibly vibrates/distorts during wind; windscreen-enclosed microphone grille remains still and undistorted; foam surface shows subtle compression-release motion; background wind indicators (e.g., grass, leaves) move synchronously.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Foam windscreens reduce wind-induced microphone diaphragm movement by dissipating turbulent airflow energy via viscous drag and flow diffusion across porous structure — preventing low-frequency rumble and handling noise.

subject: Atmospheric Science
selected_point: A cooled surface plate comes into contact with warm, moist air, forming a visible fog layer.
posted_prompt: A cold, flat metal plate placed on a table is gently blown over by warm, humid air.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Surface condensation of water vapor due to thermal contact between unsaturated warm humid air and a sub-dew-point cold surface.
Minimum mechanism: Plate temperature must be below dew point of incoming air; air must contain sufficient water vapor; surface must be thermally conductive and non-porous to enable rapid heat transfer and droplet nucleation.
(ii)Storyline: [Phase 1] Static shot: cold metal plate resting undisturbed on tabletop. [Phase 2] Airflow initiation: humid air source enters frame from side and makes contact with plate upper surface. [Phase 3] Immediate response: fog layer appears uniformly across plate surface *only during* airflow. [Phase 4] Cessation: airflow ends → fog vanishes fully within same continuous shot. [Perspective constraint] Fixed frontal/slightly angled view showing plate top surface, airflow path, and fog layer in full frame; no occlusion of contact zone; lighting enables clear differentiation of fog transparency vs. plate reflectivity.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place a clean, flat, metallic plate on a dry tabletop.
2. Generate warm, humid air (e.g., via human exhalation or humidifier nozzle) and direct it gently across the upper surface of the plate.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A thin, uniform, whitish, semi-transparent fog layer forms instantly on the plate surface during airflow and vanishes completely within 1 second after airflow stops.
Summary of Experimental Principles
When warm, moisture-laden air contacts a cooled surface, water vapor condenses into microscopic liquid droplets, forming visible fog—a phase change driven by temperature differential and surface nucleation.

pg_specification.level_1: No cold metal plate visible; no warm humid air source (e.g., no visible breath, steam plume, or fog-generating device); no tabletop surface; no demonstration of blowing action over the plate.
pg_specification.level_2: A flat metallic-looking object is present on a surface, and some airflow motion (e.g., hand movement or fan blur) occurs near it, but the object is not clearly identifiable as a cold metal plate (e.g., wrong material appearance like plastic or wood), and no visible humid air interaction is shown.
pg_specification.level_3: A flat, metallic-colored plate is placed on a tabletop; an airflow action (e.g., visible exhalation plume, misty breath, or steam-like emission) moves across the top surface of the plate; all three core objects (plate, table, humid air source) are present and spatially co-located in one continuous scene.
pg_specification.level_4: All elements from 3-score are present AND the airflow originates from a direction consistent with gentle blowing (e.g., human mouth or nozzle positioned adjacent to, not above or beneath, the plate’s upper surface); plate remains stationary throughout; no extraneous objects occlude the plate–air contact zone during airflow.
pg_specification.level_5: All elements from 4-score are present AND the humid air source is unambiguously anthropogenic (e.g., human mouth with clear lip shape and breath plume) or device-based (e.g., labeled humidifier nozzle) positioned at the side of the plate; plate has reflective metallic sheen and sharp rectangular/circular geometry; table is flat, neutral-toned, and fully supports the plate without overhang or tilt.

scc_specification.level_1: No visible condensation or fog formation on the plate; plate surface appears dry, glossy, or unchanged throughout; no state change observed between pre-airflow and airflow phases.
scc_specification.level_2: A transient visual artifact (e.g., lens flare, dust motes, or unrelated vapor) appears near the plate, but it is not localized to the plate surface and shows no adherence, persistence, or temperature-gradient correlation with airflow timing.
scc_specification.level_3: A thin, semi-transparent, whitish layer appears exclusively on the upper surface of the plate during airflow and disappears within 1 second after airflow stops; layer is continuous (not patchy or fragmented) and conforms to the plate’s shape; no liquid droplets or runoff observed.
scc_specification.level_4: All elements from 3-score are present AND the fog layer appears only after airflow begins (no pre-existing fog), persists only while airflow is active, and vanishes fully within the same continuous shot after airflow ceases; fog does not extend beyond the plate’s lateral edges or rise vertically away from the surface.
scc_specification.level_5: All elements from 4-score are present AND the fog layer exhibits uniform opacity and edge definition across the entire plate surface; no color shift (e.g., blue tint or yellow haze); no distortion, bubbling, or granular texture inconsistent with water vapor condensate; fog forms synchronously across the whole surface upon airflow onset, not sequentially from one edge.

Oxygen bubbles appear exclusively on Elodea stems only after light is restored; no bubbles form during light block.

Aquatic plant (Elodea) releases oxygen bubbles under intense light via photosynthesis; light deprivation halts O₂ production instantly.

subject: Physics
selected_point: Comparison of a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in hot water, demonstrating different rates of heat transfer
posted_prompt: Place a metal spoon and a wooden spoon side by side in the same transparent container filled with hot water, and place a small equal amount of butter on the handles of each spoon above the water surface.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Differential thermal conductivity between metal and wood drives asymmetric phase change in butter placed on spoon handles above hot water.
Minimum mechanism: Heat must propagate conductively through solid spoon material (not convectively via water or radiatively); butter phase change requires sufficient temperature rise at handle location; no external heat sources or forced convection may interfere.
(ii)Storyline: [Frame 0–2] Stable wide shot: transparent container with hot water (steam/meniscus visible); two spoons inserted side-by-side, handles aligned above water. [Frame 3–5] Butter placed simultaneously on each handle: identical size, position, orientation. [Frame 6–8] Metal spoon butter begins losing shape (edges soften, surface glistens, then pools); wooden spoon butter retains crisp geometry, no gloss or deformation. [Frame 9–10] Contrast fully established: one melted, one solid; no reversal, no ambiguity. Perspective: fixed frontal view, full spoons and waterline in frame, no occlusion, consistent lighting.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Fill a transparent container with hot water (visible steam or surface shimmer).
2. Place a metal spoon and a wooden spoon side-by-side into the water, fully submerging their bowls/shafts, with handles extending identically above water.
3. Place one small, equal portion of butter on the handle of each spoon, above water surface.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Butter on the metal spoon melts (loses solid shape, pools, or drips), while butter on the wooden spoon remains solid (retains original shape and sharp edges) throughout the observation period.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Metals conduct heat faster than wood; thermal energy transfers rapidly from hot water through the metal spoon to its handle, melting the butter. Wood is a poor conductor, so little heat reaches the wooden handle, leaving the butter unmelted.

subject: Physics
selected_point: Connect equal-length copper and iron wires into the same circuit, and verify that the bulb is brighter when using the copper wire, with a noticeable visual difference.
posted_prompt: Build a simple circuit consisting of a battery, a switch, and a light bulb. First, connect a copper wire of fixed length into the circuit and close the switch. Then replace it with an iron wire of the same length and reconnect the circuit. Clearly demonstrate the comparison process, emphasizing the correct wiring sequence and maintaining consistent conditions.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Electrical resistance determines current magnitude in a simple DC circuit, which governs bulb brightness.
Minimum mechanism: Identical voltage source, identical bulb resistance, identical wire length and cross-section, and ohmic behavior of both metals, such that resistivity difference alone causes measurable current difference and thus luminance difference.
(ii)Storyline: [0–3s] Copper wire connected; switch closed → bulb illuminates brightly and steadily. [3–4s] Switch opened; copper wire visibly removed from terminals. [4–6s] Iron wire placed onto identical terminals. [6–9s] Switch closed → bulb illuminates dimly and steadily. Throughout: fixed overhead/frontal viewpoint; bulb centered; no occlusion; consistent lighting; all connections fully visible; brightness difference immediately apparent upon switch closure in each trial.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Assemble circuit: connect battery (+) → switch → bulb → battery (−) using copper wire of fixed length.
2. Close switch; observe bulb brightness.
3. Open switch; replace copper wire with iron wire of identical length, maintaining same connection points.
4. Close switch again; observe bulb brightness.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
Bulb emits significantly brighter light with copper wire than with iron wire; brightness difference is immediate, stable, and visually unambiguous.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Copper has lower electrical resistance than iron; for equal length and cross-section, more current flows through copper, producing greater power dissipation in the bulb filament → brighter light.
